analysis.one_liner: Expands power-plant pollution trading for sulfur, nitrogen, and mercury while loosening other clean air rules.
analysis.headline: The Senate's Environment and Public Works Committee held hearings and a markup in early 2005 but never approved the bill, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the Clean Air Act's power-plant rules, replacing plant-by-plant pollution controls with national caps on sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury that utilities meet by buying and selling emission allowances. Allowances would be handed to plant owners free of charge, many units would be exempted from review required of major pollution sources, and owners could win compliance delays by claiming reliability concerns. Supporters, led by the Senate committee chairman, presented it as a reduction program; critics said it set caps lower and later than simply enforcing the existing law would have achieved.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and operators of coal- and oil-fired power plants, especially coal-heavy utilities. They would receive emission allowances at no cost each year, gain relief from major-source permitting review and hazardous-air-pollutant standards for qualifying units, and be able to delay installing control equipment through reliability petitions. The coal mining industry also benefits, since the program keeps coal-fired generation viable under a lighter regulatory regime.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal- and oil-fired power plant owners

how_it_helps.text: The bill allocates sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury allowances to plant owners at no cost, rather than auctioning them, so companies receive valuable permission-to-pollute permits for free.

Units that meet a particulate-matter limit or maintain proper control equipment are excluded from being treated as major emitting facilities, removing them from preconstruction review and regional haze requirements.
Owners or operators may petition the Secretary of Energy for a determination that pollution-control installations threaten electricity reliability, and win a compliance delay if successful.
The calculation of each unit's allowance allocation is expressly shielded from judicial review, limiting avenues for challenging how permits are apportioned.
Clean coal technology demonstration projects are exempted from performance standards and preconstruction permitting review for the pollutants whose emissions do not increase.

analysis.who_pays: People who live near and downwind of power plants. Slower and more flexible emission reductions mean continued exposure to mercury, fine particles, smog-forming nitrogen oxides, and acid-rain sulfur, with the health costs borne by communities and by children most exposed to mercury. States also give up some independent tools, since covered units get an alternative regulatory classification under the federal trading program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Downwind communities breathing power plant pollution

drawbacks.text: Allowances are allocated to owners without cost, so the bill gives away the value of the emission limits rather than collecting it for the public.
A plant that exceeds its cap can pay a penalty reduced by one third if it offsets the excess within 30 days, converting overruns into a priced option rather than a hard limit.
Owners can obtain multi-year compliance delays by petitioning the Energy Department on electricity-reliability grounds, weakening the certainty of the caps.
Exempting units from major-source review means new or modified units that meet particulate limits avoid the case-by-case air-quality analysis that otherwise applies to large pollution sources.
The bill sets national caps and deadlines stretching years into the future, so the emission reductions it promises are modest in the near term even by its own terms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is not nothing: it does impose national emission limits with per-ton penalties, monitoring requirements, and a compliance assistance fund. But the design systematically trades enforceable public-health protections for industry flexibility — free allowances, a discounted penalty for overruns, reliability-based delays, and exemptions from source-by-source review. The reductions it offers are later and smaller than what critics said existing law already required, so the main winners would be the utilities that get certainty, free permits, and protection from stricter mandates.

outcome.mechanism: After hearings in February 2005 and a committee markup in March 2005, the committee never voted the bill out and the Senate never took it up, so it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. James Inhofe, chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, introduced the bill on January 24, 2005 with Sen. George Voinovich as cosponsor, and it was referred to his own committee.
The committee held hearings on February 2, 2005.
The committee held a consideration and markup session on March 9, 2005, but the action record shows no vote reporting the bill and no further action of any kind afterward.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 with the bill still stuck in committee, so it never received a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, coal- and oil-fired power plant owners never received the free allowances, permitting exemptions, and compliance delays it offered, and downwind communities kept the existing Clean Air Act framework, which critics argued yielded stronger and faster reductions than this bill would have. Public-health and environmental groups that opposed the bill got the outcome they sought.

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.role: Chairman, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, referred it to his own committee, and brought it to hearings and a markup session.

for.name: Sen. George Voinovich
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only cosponsor.

for.name: George W. Bush administration
for.what_they_did: Originated the Clear Skies proposal in 2002 and backed its Senate introduction, with administration officials testifying at the February 2005 hearings.

for.name: Coal-fired electric utilities and coal interests
for.what_they_did: Supported the cap-and-trade framework and the relief it offered from plant-by-plant controls.

against.name: Sen. James Jeffords
against.role: Ranking Member, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Led committee opposition during the hearings and March 2005 markup, arguing the bill weakened existing Clean Air Act protections; the bill was never reported out of committee.

against.name: Sen. Lincoln Chafee
against.role: Republican member, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Broke with the chairman during the markup, joining opposition that left the committee unable to advance the bill.

against.name: Public-health and environmental groups
against.role: Advocacy organizations, including lung and children's health groups
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill, arguing its caps were weaker and later than enforcing current law and that its mercury provisions would expose children to more neurotoxic pollution for longer.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a Republican chairman's initiative with a single Republican cosponsor; the opposition that stalled it in committee came from the committee's Democrats and its one Independent, joined by one dissenting Republican.

industries.note: The bill would have made allowance trading the permanent regime for power-plant pollution, handing out free allowances annually while exempting covered units from plant-by-plant review and hazardous-pollutant standards. It regulates the industry, but on terms the industry chose, with compliance delayed and overruns priced rather than prohibited.

By extending and expanding trading programs for coal-fired generation rather than forcing specific controls at each plant, the bill would have kept coal burning viable under lighter rules, sustaining demand for mined coal.
Gentler, later pollution caps shrink the cost advantage cleaner generators hold over coal plants, and free annual allowances to fossil units transfer value to their competitors.
